stem: During pretransplant infection-prevention teaching, which animal-care activity should recipients avoid per standard references?

options.text: Cleaning aquariums, bird cages, and feeders
Walking a healthy immunized dog on a leash with routine hand hygiene afterward
Keeping household pets immunized and in good health
Following strict hand hygiene after any pet contact

explanation.rationale_correct: Animal-safety teaching includes avoiding cleaning aquariums, bird cages, and feeders, and avoiding handling fecal matter especially cat litter when possible.

rationale_incorrect.B: Routine dog walking with hand hygiene is not the activity specifically listed to avoid.
rationale_incorrect.C: Keeping pets immunized and healthy is recommended rather than avoided.
rationale_incorrect.D: Hand hygiene after pet contact is encouraged rather than avoided.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Avoid cleaning aquariums, bird cages, and feeders

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → e. Infection prevention → v. Animal safety (avoid cleaning aquariums, bird cages, and feeders); PDF p. 116 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Aquarium/bird-cage avoidance angle distinct from pet-immunization recall (cctc-1116) and animal-safety combo (cctc-1117 in batch-29); anchor verified on Cupples p. 116.

stem: An Epstein-Barr virus–seronegative candidate asks when primary Epstein-Barr virus infection most commonly occurs after transplantation. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Typically during the first 6 months post-transplant
Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection never occurs after transplantation
Only before the transplant operation with no post-transplant risk

explanation.rationale_correct: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infections occur in approximately 70% to 80% of seronegative recipients, and Epstein-Barr virus infection typically occurs during the first 6 months post-transplant.

rationale_incorrect.B: Primary infection timing is described in the early post-transplant period rather than a decade later.
rationale_incorrect.C: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection is common in seronegative recipients after transplant.
rationale_incorrect.D: Recipients may acquire primary infection from the community, allograft, or blood products after transplantation.

stem: When counseling a transplant candidate about posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD) risk, which Epstein-Barr virus factor aligns with standard references?

options.text: Undetectable Epstein-Barr virus viral load eliminates all PTLD risk
Epstein-Barr virus viral load is unrelated to PTLD
Only donor age determines Epstein-Barr virus–related PTLD risk

explanation.rationale_correct: Risk factors for PTLD include high Epstein-Barr virus viral load, primary Epstein-Barr virus infection, cytomegalovirus mismatch, and potent immunosuppression.

rationale_incorrect.B: Multiple factors beyond viral load contribute to PTLD risk.
rationale_incorrect.C: High Epstein-Barr virus viral load is specifically listed as a PTLD risk factor.
rationale_incorrect.D: Viral load and mismatch patterns are key factors rather than donor age alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Epstein-Barr virus → 3. Risk factors for PTLD

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Epstein-Barr virus → 3.b. (high EBV viral load as PTLD risk factor); PDF p. 198 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. High-EBV-viral-load risk angle distinct from EBV D+/R− mismatch (cctc-2109) and CMV mismatch (cctc-2115); anchor verified on Cupples p. 198.

stem: When explaining posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD) prevention options during evaluation, which intervention aligns with standard references?

options.text: Permanent discontinuation of all infection-prevention teaching
Routine live-virus vaccination during peak immunosuppression without planning
IVIG is contraindicated in every transplant candidate

explanation.rationale_correct: Prevention of PTLD may include Epstein-Barr virus replication inhibitors such as ganciclovir or valganciclovir and IVIG in selected cases.

rationale_incorrect.B: Infection-prevention and targeted prophylaxis remain important rather than being discontinued.
rationale_incorrect.C: Live vaccines require careful timing around immunosuppression.
rationale_incorrect.D: IVIG is listed as a preventive option rather than being universally contraindicated.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → PTLD → 5. Prevention of PTLD
